newsitem.title: CROATIA: Sick Croat leader Tudjman may quit, say diplomats.
newsitem.headline: Sick Croat leader Tudjman may quit, say diplomats.

text.p: President Franjo Tudjman has dropped from public view in Croatia, hardening suspicions that he is so ill with cancer he may have to give up his duties in a matter of months, diplomats said on Wednesday.

The 74-year-old nationalist leader, who steered Croatia to independence from Yugoslavia, was last seen more than a week ago on state-run television which usually covers his daily activities meticulously.
Tudjman on Wednesday gave his first public sign of life since December 31 when state radio reported that he met the newly appointed interior minister in the government.
He last appeared on New Year's Eve among a crowd of revellers in Zagreb's main square, sitting in a nearby cafe with his family and top government officials.

But instead of reassuring the nation that their president had rebounded from treatment in a U.S. hospital, the footage showed a pale and gaunt Tudjman and heightened speculation that his condition was rapidly deteriorating.
U.S. government sources disclosed during Tudjman's week-long stay at a Washington hospital in November that he had apparently inoperable stomach cancer and a year to live.
Western diplomats in Croatia said on Wednesday they now believed it was "a matter of months" before Tudjman is incapacitated, or possibly dead.
Recent reports in the independent media, quoting Croatian medical circles, indicate that Tudjman's health is worse than believed at first and that he only has a few months to live.
Zagreb weeklies Nacional and Globus quoted doctors as saying Tudjman was receiving daily infusions of blood, nutrients and vitamins to prevent rapid weight loss.
They also said a special suite was being prepared for him at the New Hospital in Zagreb, a former Yugoslav army clinic.
There has been no Croatian government comment on the state of Tudjman's health -- officially off-limits as a topic for discussion -- and his chief spokesman has been elusive.
Tudjman's office in the past week has confined itself to the phrase: "The president is in the country and performing his duties."
The state-dominated press kept quiet about his November trip and carried the news only after it had been broken by leading international news media.
Tudjman has no protocol duties scheduled until mid-January, when he is to receive foreign diplomats accredited in Croatia.
Analysts are debating who might replace the authoritarian helmsman who is widely regarded as "Father of the Nation".

Presidential elections are due in 1997 but analysts say they might not take place at all if Tudjman's deeply unpopular party, the Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ), decides to amend the constitution to avoid them.

The HDZ, whose popularity countrywide has slumped to some 28 percent according to the latest poll in Nacional, has no obvious presidential candidate other than Tudjman but will retain a parliamentary majority at least until 1999.
Local media say Tudjman is expected to present a draft of constitutional amendments to parliament later this month.

The draft would replace the current presidential system, in which Tudjman holds enormous power, with a more decentralised one in which the head of state would have limited authority and would be elected by parliament.

If they manage to pull it off, an HDZ president would hold power for at least two more years despite deep discontent with the party's handling of free-market reforms. The HDZ stands to lose municipal elections slated for March 16.
